meaning: Egyptian god of embalming and the necropolis; the name's etymology is uncertain (his epithet tpy-ḏw=f means He who is upon his mountain)

pronunciation.approximation: The name is a consonant skeleton: ꜣ-n-p-w; the Greeks vocalized it as Anubis.
pronunciation.note: Egyptian ꜣnpw is conventionally vocalized "Anupu" or "Anup"; the Greek rendering Anoubis gives English "Anubis." The initial ꜣ (aleph, Gardiner G1) is a glottal consonant Egyptology once ignored and now transcribes — the restoration ꜣnpw keeps the ancient consonantal skeleton exactly as the hieroglyphs write it.

domains.title: The Jackal of the Necropolis
domains.subtitle: Embalming, the Scales, and the Guiding of Souls
domains.lead: ꜣnpw is the oldest funeral god of Egypt: lord of the necropolis before Osiris ever ruled it, master of embalming, and the steady hand at the scales where every human heart is weighed against a feather. His black jackal watches from the edge of the desert where the dead were always buried.

cards.name: The Jackal
cards.desc: The desert canid seen at the graves' edge — feared for what it digs, honoured as the grave's defender.

cards.name: The Weighing
cards.desc: He steadies the scales in the Hall of Two Truths: heart against Maat's feather, exact to the grain.

cards.name: The Embalmer
cards.desc: He wrapped Osiris himself — the first mummy — and every priestly embalmer wore his mask.

cards.name: The Psychopomp
cards.desc: "Foremost of the Westerners" — guide of souls through the night roads of the dead.

symbols.name: The embalmer's mask

mythology.lead: In the earliest religion ꜣnpw simply is the god of the dead; when the Osiris cycle rose, he was written into it — as embalmer, son, and guide — without ever losing his seniority at the grave.

myths.title: The First Embalming
myths.text: Isis had gathered all the pieces of Osiris' body that Set had scattered — save one, swallowed by a fish of the Nile — when ꜣnpw came to perform the rite no god had yet done. He washed the god's flesh, anointed it with oils, wrapped it in fine linen and breathed the first funerary formula over it: the first mummy, and the template of every burial Egypt would ever perform (Plutarch, De Iside et Osiride 13–14; the older Pyramid Texts already call ꜣnpw 'he who is upon his mountain', watcher of the god's booth). In temple ritual the connection stayed literal for three thousand years: the chief embalmer, the 'overseer of the mysteries', wore the jackal mask, so that the hands wrapping the dead were visibly Anubis' own. The myth makes the funerary craft a divine inheritance: mummification is not technique applied to religion but religion continued by technique.

myths.title: The Feather of Maat
myths.text: Spell 125 of the Book of the Dead — whose vignettes multiply from the Eighteenth Dynasty onward — fixes his most famous office. In the Hall of the Two Truths the deceased recites the Negative Confession, forty-two denials of sin before forty-two judges; then ꜣnpw, he who counts the hearts, leads the dead to the scales and steadies the beam while the heart is weighed against the single feather of Maat. Thoth records the verdict; a heart heavy with lies tips the pan, and Ammit the Devourer — crocodile's head, lion's foreparts, hippopotamus' hindquarters — waits beside the scales to eat it, annihilating the sinner's afterlife. A true-of-voice heart passes on to Horus and Osiris. That the terrible reading of the scales belongs to the jackal-god is the theology in one image: the watcher at the desert's edge, feared in life as a digger among bodies, is in death the incorruptible accountant of souls.

myths.title: The Hidden Child of Osiris
myths.text: The genealogy is late and layered. In the Old Kingdom texts ꜣnpw simply is — lord of the necropolis before any family attached. Later traditions tried to attach him: one strand makes him son of the cow-goddess Hesat, and the story preserved by Plutarch (De Iside et Osiride 12, 14) makes him the secret child of Osiris and Nephthys — conceived while Set was away, hidden in the marshes for shame, found and raised by Isis. Plutarch's is the version that stuck, and its pathos is real: the god of the embalming-table as the concealed child of the very body he would wrap. But scholars note the direction of the theology: it was written backwards, from his office to his family. The hidden child of a murder is set, for eternity, to repairing that murder — lineage as job description.

myths.title: He Who Is Upon His Mountain
myths.text: His Old Kingdom titles read like a map of the necropolis: jmy-wt, 'he who is in the place of embalming'; ḫnty-sḥ-nṯr, 'foremost of the divine booth'; ḫnty-jmntjw, 'foremost of the Westerners' — the dead, who live where the sun goes down; and tpy-ḏw=f, 'he who is upon his mountain', the watcher on the ridge above the graves. On Middle Kingdom coffins and later tomb walls he leans over the bier, one black paw resting gently on the mummy — not a threat but an escort. No soul reaches the Field of Reeds unaccompanied: spells of the Book of the Dead equip the dead to travel in his retinue, and he leads the justified through the night roads of the Duat. The theology is consistent across three millennia: death is a border crossing, and the border is his.

lore.syncretism: The Greeks, finding a jackal-headed guide of souls, fused him at once with Hermês: Hermanubis — kerykeion in one paw, jackal head on his shoulders — received cult at Alexandria and in Rome, an identification so natural that Coptic speakers simply called the god-form Anoup. In the Isiac mysteries he served as mystagogue: Apuleius, initiated at Cenchreae, describes the grand procession in which Anubis, herald and messenger 'between the gods above and the gods below', walked before the goddess in gold and black (Metamorphoses 11.11). Early Coptic Christianity quietly absorbed his office into the archangel Michael — weigher and guide of souls — so that a jackal-god of the third millennium BCE ended, unbroken, as an angel with scales. Egyptomania later restored him to European consciousness through Belzoni's exhibitions and the decipherment of the hieroglyphs.
lore.culturalLegacy: He is, for most of the world, the face of ancient Egypt: Tutankhamun's recumbent jackal shrine — black wood, gilded ears, guarding the royal canopic chest — is among the most reproduced objects on earth, and the mummy-genre of cinema, from Karloff's Imhotep to modern franchises, works entirely in his territory. The modern image of justice borrowed his instrument: every balanced beam in courthouse iconography unconsciously quotes his scales. Egyptology has spent two centuries correcting the horror-movie caricature — feared on screen as a monster, he was antiquity's most trusted guardian, the gentle final attendant of every Egyptian who could afford the rite. His jackal still patrols the edge of the desert at Saqqara, exactly where the watchers always stood.
lore.extendedMeditation:
ꜣnpw is the god of careful hands. At the two moments a human being is most helpless — the body's unmaking and the heart's examination — he is the one present who touches gently and reads honestly. Civilizations, the Egyptians believed, are judged by how they treat their dead; he is the god of that judgment in both senses, and his cult turned a despised trade into sacred office: the embalmers, the 'pure ones', served him.

His animal is the lesson. The desert canid digs at graves; the Egyptians saw it nightly at the desert's edge, doing exactly what everyone feared. The myth's answer was not to banish the fear but to enlist it: make the grave-digger the grave-guardian, the feared thing the trustworthy one. Few religions have made a cleaner statement about fear itself — that it is a power, and powers are better consecrated than denied.

lore.archaeology: Tutankhamun's tomb (KV62) yielded the Anubis shrine: a life-size black wooden jackal, gilded ears and collar, guarding the canopic equipment — now in Cairo. The Anubeion at Saqqara, excavated over decades, preserves catacombs of mummified dogs and jackals offered to him — estimates run to millions of animals across Egypt's canine catacombs. Vignettes of spell 125, with his hand on the scales, survive in hundreds of Books of the Dead, from the papyrus of Ani in the British Museum to the papyrus of Hunefer.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is written ꜣ-n-p-w with the recumbent jackal (Gardiner E16) as determinative, over the hotep offering sign in the fuller orthographies. The Greeks heard it as Anoubis; Coptic preserved it as Anoup. The jackal is not decorative: it is the god himself, present in his own spelling.
